comparator.name: Plant Sciences
comparator.sourceNotes: Current BPW Plant Production and Ecology pathway:105 compulsory taught +3 conditional mathematics/statistics +24 specialisation +18 thesis +30 genuinely open credits =180. First-year compulsory57 plus conditional3 =60; B2 common48 plus route12 =60; B3 route12 plus thesis18 plus open30 =60. The separately credited Introduction8, Ecology3 and Crop Recognition2 have distinct current course identities/content/assessments; their coordinated first-period scheduling is not a parent/child credit duplication. Three safety courses carry zero credits. MAT14803 is prescribed for Mathematics A preparation, not chosen by source-order tie-break; MAT15303 applies to Mathematics B. The selected introduction is in B1 period2 first-half morning before Statistics2 in the second half; school statistics provides its stated preparation, while later Analysis/Linear Algebra follow the introduction. Complete all132 prescribed taught credits and obtain coordinator permission before YPS82318. Current module/handbook rules are sufficient; an unavailable historical guide is not used to supply missing requirements. No named minor, extra safety/reflection credit or second specialisation is invented.
components: An 8-credit introduction with disciplinary case studies, field/lab activity and academic development. The written tests and group report each require a passing mark; the personal development plan and information-literacy work must also pass. General, laboratory and fieldwork safety are additional zero-credit requirements.

A separate 2-credit course in identifying crop species and products. Attendance, workbook/excursion and longitudinal assignments must be completed, and the recognition test must pass; this is distinct from the introductory course.
General Chemistry for the Life Sciences

Includes ecological field data, a group-designed greenhouse experiment, presentations, company/institution visits and interviews with three plant-science professionals. Reflection must pass; presentations require a sufficient combined result and minimum marks for their components.
Biology and Management of Plant Pests and Diseases
Resilience in Plant Sciences: Integrated Research from Molecules to Agro-Ecosystems

A 12-credit integrated research course. Students conduct a project in pairs, write an individual scientific paper, and work across molecular-to-agroecosystem perspectives on a resilience case. The paper and group case each require a passing mark; individual reflection must also pass.

The 3-credit choice depends on prior mathematics: this example takes Mathematics Applied: Introduction for Mathematics A preparation. Students with Mathematics B take Statistics 1. Statistics 2 assumes active school statistics or Statistics 1.
Agricultural Ecosystems - Linking Ecology, Agronomy & Rural Realities
Physiology and Development of Plants in Agriculture

Required 18-credit individual plant-science research project: proposal, experiments, data analysis, written report, oral presentation, discussion and reflection/future study plan. Entry requires coordinator permission and at least 102 prescribed credits, including all first-year credits. This example completes all 132 prescribed taught credits before the thesis; permission remains a requirement.

Thirty open credits remain for a minor and/or individual electives. Seagriculture, Experimental Plant Sciences and Resilient Crops are optional minors, not additional compulsory specialisations; no particular minor is assumed.

routeSelection.basis: Retain Plant Production and Ecology as the neutral broad-identity choice: the current programme describes plant/environment interactions, physiology, ecology, agronomy, agroecology, farming systems and technological responses across plant-to-agroecosystem scales. Plant Genomics and Health concentrates more narrowly on cellular/molecular processes. This external-route choice is independent of UCR fit; it does not select an optional minor.

alternatives.label: Biology, agroecology & environmental resilience
alternatives.labelReason: Investigate biological and ecological mechanisms relevant to plants and sustainable agricultural systems. Combine cellular/biochemical foundations with biodiversity, farming practices, soil and water processes, climate pressures and quantitative inquiry. Specialist crop physiology and cultivation remain substantial differences.
alternatives.concept: Investigate biological and ecological mechanisms relevant to plants and sustainable agricultural systems. progression: All formal prerequisites occur in earlier semesters and every assigned term is planned. Biological and chemical gateways precede later cellular/biochemical/laboratory and environmental work. Cell Biology precedes molecular pathology/genetics in the molecular route; basic statistics/design precedes advanced analysis. Soil science and ecology support farming applications, and introductory economics/sociology precede later policy/qualitative work where feasible. No extra hard prerequisites invented.

selection.assessment: First reconstruct the strongest biological/ecological response using actual cell/biochemical, biodiversity, farming, soil/water and quantitative content, rather than human physiology or clinical immunity. Then accept a distinct molecular/laboratory/computational response after removing the former neuroscience organising weight. Then accept an ecological farming/resource-policy response: six courses apart from the closest route, with actual farming/environmental science and specific economic/qualitative/policy methods. Pairwise differences are8/6/13 courses,60/45/97.5EC. The organising priorities precede selection and were checked for programme-level response, not coherence alone. Stop at three; remaining optional-minor directions are not automatically extra specialisations. Major plant physiology, crop recognition/reproduction/breeding, pest management and specialist greenhouse/field/research depth remain explicit limits.

trace: Direct molecular/cellular, DNA/heredity, genome and biochemical foundations support life-science reasoning. The course analyses published experiments; no hands-on laboratory or plant-specific physiology is invented.

Direct organismal diversity, plant/fungal groups, phylogeny, identification and biodiversity measurement establish a real botanical/ecological foundation. Broad organism identification is not specialised crop/product recognition.

Direct chemical equilibria, thermodynamic principles, mechanics, dynamic models and biopolymer preparation supply chemical/physical tools and a plant-derived material example. Sustainability framing is not a plant physiology course.

Direct reproducible R-based cleaning, integration, exploration and visualisation of tabular/spatial/text data supply research-data methods. The student project uses a field of interest; plant data is not guaranteed.

Direct eukaryotic cellular mechanisms, membranes, signalling, genome replication/regulation and bioenergetics support cellular explanations relevant across organisms. The drug-target project is not a plant experiment or crop physiology course.

Direct calculus, differential equations, numerical approximation and dynamic-model implementation supply quantitative tools for ecological and biological inquiry; no guaranteed crop simulation project.

Direct empirical/experimental design, measurement, sampling, introductory inference/regression and R analysis support planning and interpreting biological/social research; the survey/project is not a compulsory plant experiment.

Direct biomolecular structure, enzymes, kinetics, regulation and carbon/lipid/nitrogen metabolism support biochemical mechanisms. Its disease literature project is not plant-pathogen work, organic synthesis or a cell-to-canopy photosynthesis sequence.

Complementary rocks, minerals, sediments, geological history and field observation establish the substrate/landscape basis for soils. The Ardennes mapping project is geological, not an agricultural field trial.

Direct climate drivers/feedbacks, agricultural/ecosystem impacts and adaptation/mitigation support climate-resilience analysis. Stakeholder communication is a specific complementary method, not a crop stress experiment.

Direct experimental design and applied multivariable/categorical, regression, repeated-measures and factor analyses in R support rigorous experimental data interpretation. The course is health/behaviour-oriented; methods transfer does not promise plant data.

Direct organism-population-community-ecosystem ecology, resources, competition, population dynamics and energy/matter cycles support agroecosystem reasoning. R-based ecological modelling and a research poster add actual analytical methods.

Direct wave/optical methods, chemical testing and material structure/behaviour supply physical and chemical investigation tools. Actual sustainability case analysis does not become plant transformation or greenhouse engineering.

Direct soil formation, texture/structure, moisture, organic matter, pH, biology and salinization support assessment of soil environments. Field/lab soil measurements are real; root physiology and crop nutrition remain broader at WUR, while UCR also includes aquifer geophysics.

Direct linear systems, differential/difference representations, transforms, sampling/filtering and feedback supply analytical tools for dynamical models and experimental signals; no nonlinear crop-system or plant-physiology equivalence.

Direct Mendelian/population/quantitative genetics, variation/selection, evolutionary genomics, development and phylogeny support plant genetic diversity and adaptation. The species-history project is not crop domestication or breeding practice.

Direct aqueous equilibria, speciation, carbonate/redox chemistry, adsorption and mineral/biological processes explain nutrient/contaminant environments. Geochemical modelling, laboratory evidence and remediation applications are not crop physiological experimentation.

Direct probability, estimation/testing, Bayesian methods and Monte Carlo computation support inference, sampling and uncertainty in biological/environmental research. This is not the full applied R regression/ANOVA course.

Direct phytoremediation/mycoremediation and mycelium/soil-amendment work provides an actual plant/microbial environmental application. Leaching, material separation, metal analysis and protocol design add chemical experimental skills; the full course is resource recovery, not plant breeding or a plant research capstone.

Direct biodiversity threats, habitat fragmentation, invasive species, climate impacts and conservation in human-modified landscapes support biodiversity-sensitive land use. Its threatened-species project is not guaranteed agricultural or plant-specific.

Direct microbial culture, transformation, protein purification, DNA/PCR, electrophoresis, bioinformatics and reproducible records provide experimental biological methods. Blood/microbial/protein/DNA work does not become crop breeding, plant transformation or greenhouse research.

Direct agricultural/horticultural systems, farming impacts, biodiversity, alternative practices and innovation supply the main farming contribution. Its comparative literature project evaluates sustainable-farming evidence; no practical cultivation, crop-growth model or on-farm measurement is invented.

Direct institutions/actors, collective action, food/water/energy governance, stakeholder analysis and policy effectiveness supply a bounded decision framework for sustainable farming and resource transitions. It is sustainability governance, not crop science.
Direct Python programming, structured/recursive problem solving, testing and debugging enable scientific data/model implementations; no domain-specific plant software is promised.
Direct vectors, matrices, eigenvalues, least squares and matrix dynamics support quantitative biological models and multivariable data methods.

Direct numerical root finding, quadrature, ODEs, linear/nonlinear systems and accuracy/stability analysis support scientific simulation. Numerical techniques are real, but ecological model construction/calibration and crop-system cases are not guaranteed.

Direct inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, gene regulation and DNA technologies provide a general genetic mechanism perspective. Human pathology and the grant-proposal setting remain explicit; plant gene editing, defence and breeding are not claimed.

Direct drug-target action, kinetics/metabolism, toxicity and quantitative drug responses give a complementary perspective on bioactive molecules and health applications. The course neither studies extraction/biosynthesis of plant metabolites nor develops plant medicines.

The official description supports multidimensional calculus, differential equations, complex-valued functions and computer algebra for quantitative science. No absent outline topic or specialised plant model is invented.

Direct image filtering, segmentation, features and recognition pipelines in Python/OpenCV supply tools applicable to biological images. The actual recognition project is not promised to study crops or greenhouse phenotyping.

Direct neural-network implementation, training, validation and computer-vision/time-series methods supply modern research-computing tools. Tabular/image/text projects are not guaranteed plant datasets, and predictive models are not mechanistic crop physiology.
Markets, incentives, consumer choice, costs and basic economic models provide foundations for resource/production decisions; not agricultural-economics specialisation.
Complementary institutions, inequality and social problems provide concepts for farming livelihoods, resource access and food-system trade-offs; not agronomy.

Direct delta freshwater scarcity, salinization, drainage, water quality and adaptation trade-offs supply a water-resource context for farming. Site-based water appraisal is not crop production training.

Direct public goods, externalities, efficiency/equity, public spending and model-based policy appraisal support analysis of environmental and food-system resource trade-offs. Health/welfare examples are not relabelled crop-production content.

Direct qualitative design, stakeholder interviews/focus groups, observation, coding and reflexivity support understanding farming/resource decisions. The general project is not guaranteed agricultural.

The official description supports policy-making phases, alternative conceptualisations, a sugar case across national/international arenas and policy memos. This provides concrete policy-analysis tools; no missing methods or agricultural-policy specialisation invented.

notes.text: WUR builds sustained expertise in plant structure and physiology, crop recognition and reproduction, breeding, pests and diseases, cultivation, and plant-specific field, greenhouse and experimental research. These UCR programmes offer related biological, ecological, molecular, environmental and analytical perspectives, with substantial gaps in that specialist plant-science sequence.

audience.programmeDescription: WUR’s Dutch-taught Plant Sciences bachelor studies how plants function and interact with their environment, from cells and genes to crops and agroecosystems. It combines biological research with applications to food production, health, renewable resources and environmental resilience.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The first UCR programme connects biological mechanisms with ecology, farming and soil-environment study. The second emphasises molecular, laboratory and computational methods; the third focuses on sustainable farming and resource-policy decisions. WUR provides substantially more plant physiology, crop recognition, breeding, pest management and specialist greenhouse/field research. Its 18-credit thesis is required; UCR’s optional independent research is additional to the illustrated 180 credits.
